newsitem.title: CAMBODIA: Cambodia must act after setting poll date -analyst.
newsitem.headline: Cambodia must act after setting poll date -analyst.

text.p: Cambodia has set a date for general elections but the announcement must be followed by swift legislative and administrative preparations, political analysts said on Tuesday.
First Prime Minister Prince Norodom Ranariddh and his uneasy coalition partner, Hun Sen, agreed the election should be held next May, Ranariddh said.

The United Nations sponsored Cambodia's first democratic elections in 1993, at a cost of $2 billion for an 18-month peacekeeping mission, in an attempt to shake off two decades of warfare, foreign intervention and the "killing fields" rule of the dreaded Khmer Rouge.

Now a bitter power struggle between Ranariddh and Hun Sen and a row over how to deal with Khmer Rouge leader Pol Pot and his unravelling rebel base has crippled the coalition and deadlocked the national assembly, preventing the passing of key electoral laws.
Analysts said the pair had drawn their own road map and now had to be seen to be moving quickly in the right direction.
"I think it's a good thing they're committed to a date," said a foreign political analyst. "Before...there was much less need to push through the needed legislation.
"Action is going to need to take place, and to be seen to take place -- starting now," he said.
"We have to start now," said Kao Kim Hourn, director of the Cambodian Institute for Cooperation and Peace think tank. "If we wait two or three months it will be too late."
Lao Mong Hay, director of the Khmer Institute of Democracy, said international pressure on the leaders of the fractured coalition was needed to ensure the elections were held.
"The parliamentary machine has ground to a halt," he said. "We need pressure from the international community.
"Now that they've fixed a date, after that, our government, our parliament, will be losing legitimacy and the right to rule (if preparations for the election are not made)," he said.

Ranariddh's announcement came just days before U.S. Secretary of State Madeleine Albright was due in Cambodia for a scheduled visit. It also followed a call by the Group of Seven and Russia to the country's leaders to demonstrate their commitment to democracy.
Albright was due to visit Cambodia later this month but the U.S. State Department later said she was reconsidering her trip in the light of security concerns.
Last week bodyguards loyal to the two prime ministers fought a brief but fierce gun battle on the streets of Phnom Penh.
The government played down the clash, which left two of Ranariddh's men dead, as an isolated incident but political sources said it illustrated the potential for explosive political violence.
Ranariddh said the election was more important for the impoverished country than the capture of Pol Pot which has made headlines around the world.
"Pol Pot is past...for me the elections are much more important," he said.
The Khmer Rouge reneged on a 1991 peace pact and kept up a low-intensity war against the coalition government formed after the 1993 polls.
More than one million Cambodians died of starvation, disease or hard labour, or were executed as enemies of the Khmer Rouge during their 1975-79 reign of terror.
